name: Citrullinaemia type 2 (citrin deficiency)
aliases: NICCD (neonatal intrahepatic cholestasis caused by citrin deficiency)

reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Caused by biallelic SLC25A13 variants affecting citrin, the mitochondrial aspartate-glutamate carrier, not a urea cycle enzyme itself
Age-dependent phenotypes: neonatal cholestasis (NICCD), a childhood failure-to-thrive/dyslipidaemic stage, and adult-onset citrullinaemia (CTLN2)
NICCD presents with intrahepatic cholestasis, galactosuria, hypoproteinaemia and often self-limited jaundice in infancy
Adult CTLN2 causes recurrent hyperammonaemic encephalopathy with neuropsychiatric symptoms, often precipitated by alcohol, medication or carbohydrate load
A striking clue is a self-selected diet rich in protein and fat with an aversion to carbohydrates and sweets
Biochemistry shows raised citrulline and ammonia with an elevated arginine and abnormal threonine-to-serine ratio; pancreatic secretory trypsin inhibitor (PSTI) may be raised
Confirmed by SLC25A13 sequencing; the disorder is especially prevalent in East Asian populations

High-carbohydrate treatment is harmful; management favours a low-carbohydrate, higher-protein/fat diet, avoidance of glycerol/high-glucose infusions, arginine and nitrogen scavengers, with liver transplantation for severe CTLN2
reference.pathophysiology: Citrullinaemia type 2 is caused by deficiency of citrin, the liver-type mitochondrial aspartate-glutamate carrier encoded by SLC25A13, a component of the malate-aspartate shuttle. Citrin exports aspartate from mitochondria to the cytosol, where aspartate is required by argininosuccinate synthetase to combine with citrulline in the urea cycle and for the shuttle that transfers reducing equivalents (NADH) into mitochondria. Loss of citrin therefore both limits cytosolic aspartate for ureagenesis, causing citrulline accumulation and hyperammonaemia, and impairs the malate-aspartate shuttle, raising the cytosolic NADH:NAD ratio and disturbing carbohydrate/lipid metabolism. This explains the characteristic carbohydrate intolerance, the harm from glucose loading, and the preference for protein- and fat-rich foods. Inheritance is autosomal recessive.
additionalDifferentials: Other urea cycle disorders with hyperammonaemia
Neonatal cholestasis of other cause (biliary atresia, infection, other metabolic liver disease)
Alcohol-related or hepatic encephalopathy in adults
Psychiatric illness (for the neuropsychiatric CTLN2 presentation)
Galactosaemia and other causes of neonatal galactosuria
additionalInvestigations: Plasma ammonia and plasma amino acids (raised citrulline, arginine; abnormal threonine/serine)
Liver function tests and coagulation in cholestatic infants
Plasma and urine galactose/galactitol in NICCD
Serum pancreatic secretory trypsin inhibitor where available
Fasting lipid profile and glucose tolerance assessment
Brain imaging in adults with encephalopathy to exclude other causes
redFlags: Adult hyperammonaemic encephalopathy with rapid neurological decline
Cerebral oedema during a CTLN2 crisis
Precipitation of coma by high-carbohydrate/glucose infusion or glycerol
Progressive cholestatic liver failure in an affected infant
Recurrent unexplained neuropsychiatric episodes with hyperammonaemia
reference.prognosis: NICCD usually resolves with supportive care and appropriate feeding, but adult CTLN2 can be life-threatening with recurrent hyperammonaemic crises and may require liver transplantation; dietary management markedly influences outcome.
pitfalls: Giving high-glucose or glycerol-containing infusions, which can precipitate or worsen a crisis
Applying a standard high-carbohydrate, protein-restricted urea-cycle diet, which is counterproductive here
Misattributing adult encephalopathy to alcohol or psychiatric disease and missing citrin deficiency
Overlooking NICCD as a cause of neonatal cholestasis
Ignoring the diagnostic clue of carbohydrate aversion and protein/fat preference
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease (OMMBID)
Saudubray, Inborn Metabolic Diseases: Diagnosis and Treatment
management: A carbohydrate-restricted, protein- and fat-rich diet with medium-chain triglycerides as the mainstay, in keeping with the patient's spontaneous food preference
Avoidance of glucose loading and of glycerol- or fructose-containing infusions, which can precipitate deterioration in this condition
Supportive management of neonatal intrahepatic cholestasis with a medium-chain-triglyceride and fat-soluble-vitamin-supplemented formula
Avoidance of adult crisis triggers such as alcohol, certain medications and high carbohydrate intake
Acute hyperammonaemic encephalopathy managed with nitrogen-scavenging agents and arginine while avoiding glucose overload, with haemodialysis for refractory elevation
Monitoring of plasma ammonia and amino acids, liver function and the lipid profile over time
Liver transplantation for recurrent life-threatening hyperammonaemic crises
Genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive SLC25A13 disorder with family testing
